Both, the Present Perfect and the Past Simple, help us to communicate in an accurate way about different events in the past.

PRESENT PERFECT

Remember that the Present Perfect tense makes reference to events that started in the past and that continue until the moment of speaking. Furthermore, we do not know when the action will finish in the future.

  • For affirmative sentences, use the auxiliary verb “have” or “has” depending on the subject of the sentence. Plus, change the form of the verb to the past participle one.
  • For negative sentences, use the negative form of the auxiliary verb “have” or “has” and keep the verb in its past participle form.
  • For interrogative sentences,follow he structure (WH- question word) + have/has + subject + verb (past participle form) + complement + ?.

PAST SIMPLE

The Past Simple is used to talk about actions that started and finished at a specific moment in the past.

  • For affirmative sentences, just change the form of the verb depending on its type, regular or irregular.
  • For negative sentences, use the negative form of the auxiliary verb “did” (did not or didn’t) and keep the verb in its base form.

For interrogative form,use the structure (WH- question word) + did + subject + verb (base form) + complement + ?.

Used To and Would - Negative Forms
Both used to and would, refer to a past habit; in other words, a recurrent action in the past that no longer happens in the present.

USED TO

The negative form of this structure is “did not use to + main verb (infinitive)”. In this case, you are expressing that a certain activity was not a habit in someone’s or something’s past. 

Examples:

We didn’t use to use that database in my last job.

She didn’t use to be so knowledgeable about databases.

WOULD

The negative form of “would” for past habits is really easy since it is only required to add the adverb “not” after it and a main verb in the infinitive form.

Examples:

In my last job, we wouldn’t use that database.

Five years ago, she would not be so knowledgeable about this.

First of all, I didn't use to work alone in one single project and I would normally be accompanied by other five coworkers who wouldn't do other things different than help me finish all the data validation processes on time.
Well, in my case, the situation didn't use to be different from yours when I worked. However, I wouldn't feel as bad as you.

Frank: This week is finally over. You cannot imagine how many issues I’ve had with the project we started this semester. It’s been a disaster.

Liana: Really? What happened? Have you talked to your boss about that?

Frank: First of all, I didn’t use to work alone in one single project and I would normally be accompanied by other five coworkers who wouldn’t do other things different than help me finish all the data validation processes on time. That is why I have worked all week on my own fixing the human mistakes that all the members of a company made when they registered their clients’ information.

Liana: What type of mistakes did you find?

Frank: I didn’t find but spelling mistakes and incomplete required fields. I remember that I didn’t use to have to face these types of problematic situations before. Now, my job has become really dull.

Liana: Well, in my case, the situation didn’t use to be different from yours when I worked. However, I wouldn’t feel as bad as you because I always attempted to use as many techniques and methods as I could to maximize my data validation processes. Whenever I was in charge of any of those projects, I would not hesitate to use early versions of the field level and the form level validations as they would prevent those mistakes from happening. Obviously, there were some other mistakes that did not use to be covered by those types of validations but, anyways, the workload wouldn’t be so hefty. 

Frank: I didn’t think about that before. Now that I think about that, I haven’t managed this situation in the appropriate way. Thank you for the advice.
